items.text: Argentina’s President, Javier Milei, is marking his first year in office with significant economic and social reforms. He implemented one of the country’s strictest austerity plans, cutting public works, subsidies, and state jobs while devaluing the currency by 50%. Inflation has been the lowest in years, but these measures have also deepened poverty and unemployment. At least half of Argentina’s population now lives in poverty, and many struggle to afford basic needs. Supporters highlight his achievements in stabilizing the economy and reducing spending. Some people praise him for introducing laws to modernize the economy and attract foreign investment. Critics argue that his reforms harm the most vulnerable. Milei’s popularity remains high among those hoping his policies will lead to long-term growth, but others feel his approach favors the wealthy and leaves many Argentinians behind. Difficult words: austerity (strict measures to reduce spending), devalue (to reduce the worth or importance of), favor (to support or prefer one particular possibility or group). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Javier Milei is celebrating his first year as Argentina’s President. He introduced economic measures to lower inflation and stabilize the economy. These included cutting public jobs and reducing subsidies for services like transport and electricity. While inflation dropped, over half the population didn’t have enough money even for food. Some people believe that Milei’s reforms will fix the country’s problems and bring foreign money. Other people say that these changes only help rich people and hurt the poor. Although Milei’s plans may help Argentina grow in the future, many people feel that they don’t get enough help from the government. Difficult words: measure (a plan or action which someone takes to achieve something), stabilize (to make something stable), subsidy (money the government gives to help pay for something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Javier Milei is Argentina’s President. He is in office for one year. He makes big changes to fix the country’s economy. He cuts jobs and reduces government help for things like transport and electricity. These changes stop prices from rising quickly. But many people become poorer . Some people like Milei’s work. They think that his ideas will help Argentina in the future. Others say that his changes only help rich people and hurt the poor. In Buenos Aires, many families do not have enough food. Many people hope things will get better. But life is very hard for now. Difficult words: reduce (to make things smaller or less important), poor (when you do not have enough money), rich (when you have a lot of money). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Health officials are warning people to stop using e-cigarettes, as the number of illnesses related to them continues to rise in the United States. The health officials said that they know about 450 cases across 33 states of illnesses possibly related to e-cigarettes. That is more than double the number of cases reported two weeks ago. The number of deaths due to lung injury has also increased to five cases since August this year. The officials said that it is too early to say what exact chemical in the e-cigarettes is causing the problems because some patients reported smoking both e-cigarettes and marijuana. Some reported using nicotine only. The officials advise e-cigarette users not to buy e-cigarettes in the streets, as well as not to add any substances that are not intended by the manufacturer. Difficult words: due to (thanks to), cause (be the reason for something), intend (plan). You can watch the original video news lower on this page.

Health officials say that it is important to be careful when people use e-cigarettes. The number of illnesses connected to e-cigarettes continues to go up in the United States. Health officials say that they know about 450 possible cases of illnesses in 33 states. These cases can be connected to e-cigarettes. This number is two times higher than the number two weeks ago, and five people already died in the last two months. The officials say that they do not know exactly what chemical is in the e-cigarettes that is the reason for the problems. Some people smoked e-cigarettes and also marijuana, but some people smoked only e-cigarettes. The officials say that it is better to use only products which people buy in stores and not in the streets. Difficult words: official (a leader, a boss), case (a person who has some illness). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Health officials say that e-cigarettes can be a problem. More and more people are sick from them in the United States. The health officials say that they know about 450 sick people. These people use e-cigarettes. Five of these people die. The officials do not know what chemical is in the e-cigarettes. They do not know what chemical is making people sick. Some people also smoke marijuana in e-cigarettes. The officials say that it is better to use only products from stores and not from the streets. Difficult words: health (situation in your body), officials (people who are bosses), chemical (a thing which is inside of other things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Romania’s highest court has canceled the ongoing presidential election following accusations of interference by Russia. The election must now be restarted. It featured a contest between far-right, pro-Russian candidate Calin Georgescu and pro-European centrist Elena Lasconi. Before November’s first round of voting, Georgescu had low support in polls but surprisingly finished first, raising concerns about the election’s validity . Georgescu called the court’s decision a coup , while Lasconi condemned it as illegal and harmful to democracy. If elected, Georgescu’s presidency could shift Romania closer to Russia-friendly politics, challenging its pro-European and NATO stance . Romania’s security council revealed Russian hybrid attacks targeted the election, prompting an investigation into Georgescu’s campaign. Russia denies any involvement. President Klaus Iohannis will extend his term until a new vote occurs, possibly in March 2025. Citizens expressed frustration over the court’s decision, but parliamentary results from December were unaffected. Difficult words: validity (being valid or reasonable), coup (an unexpected achievement), stance (a publicly stated opinion). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Romania’s top court stopped the presidential election after accusations of Russian influence. The election began and was meant to finish soon. Far-right candidate Calin Georgescu, who supports Russia, was competing against pro-European Elena Lasconi. Georgescu won the first round, which caused doubts about the results. He called the court’s decision a success, but Lasconi said it was bad for democracy. Romania’s security council said Russia targeted the election with special attacks, and an investigation started. Russia denies this. President Klaus Iohannis will be in office possibly until March 2025. People are unhappy with the court’s decision. Parliamentary elections from December will stay the same. Difficult words: accusation (saying that someone did something wrong), doubt (feeling unsure about something), to deny (saying that something is not true). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Romania’s top court cancels its presidential election . It is possible that Russia is trying to change the result of the election. Calin Georgescu is a far-right candidate who likes Russia. The other candidate is Elena Lasconi. She likes the EU. Georgescu is not popular at first but wins. People have questions about the result. Georgescu says that the court is not fair. Romania says that Russia wants to change the election with attacks. Russia says this is not true. Romania’s president will stay until new elections happen, maybe in March 2025. People in Romania are upset . Difficult words: presidential election (when people vote for a new president), result (how something ends), upset (unhappy, nervous). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

According to the magazine ‘Psychology Today’, a hobby is important for people for many reasons. Firstly, a hobby structures your time because you have to make time for the hobby. Secondly, the hobby rejuvenates you when you lose yourself in focusing on the activity. Thirdly, it relieves stress from your daily life. Fourthly, you are more social as you meet people who do the same hobby, and you also become more interesting if you do more activities. The sixth reason is the hobby’s effects on the brain. Your brain gets efficient as you do your hobby or learn new skills. The new skill turns on the brain’s neurons to make more connections, and thus you learn quicker and slow down ageing. You also increase the material in the brain that keeps it working well. Having a hobby can change your life in many ways! Difficult words: rejuvenate (to make you seem younger, to give you energy), lose yourself (when you focus only on what you are doing; you do not notice time passing), neurons (the connections in the brain that send signals to make the brain work). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A psychology magazine wrote about why a hobby is important for people. Firstly, it gives you structured time. Secondly, it can rejuvenate you. Thirdly, it lowers your stress . Fourthly, you meet more people who also do the hobby. Fifthly, you are more interesting when you do more activities. The sixth reason is what the hobby does to the brain: the brain grows and works better because you are learning a new skill. You learn faster and slow down ageing . The brain also grows more material to keep it working well. Having a hobby helps your life in many ways! Difficult words: rejuvenate (give you energy), stress (the body’s reaction to difficult situations), ageing (getting older). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A psychology magazine writes about why it is good to have a hobby . First, it gives you structured time . Secondly, doing a hobby can give you energy. Thirdly, hobbies can make you less stressed. Fourthly, you meet new people who also do the hobby. Fifthly, you are more interesting when you do more activities. The sixth reason helps the brain. The brain grows. It works better from the new skill . You learn faster. This slows down the process of getting older. The brain also grows more material. This material keeps it working well. Having a hobby helps your life in many ways! Difficult words: hobby (an activity that you do for fun), structured time (time where you have to work on the hobby), skill (a hobby; an activity that you are good or you enjoy). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad has fled Damascus as rebel forces entered the city, ending decades of his rule. The insurgents declared Damascus free just two weeks after a rapid offensive that began in northern Syria. According to reports, the Syrian army notified officers of the regime’s collapse. Prime Minister Mohammed al-Jal-Ali announced he was ready to support a peaceful transfer of power to a leader chosen by the people. The rebels, advancing from multiple directions, freed prisoners and encountered minimal opposition. Many Syrian soldiers retreated or fled to Iraq. Assad’s whereabouts remain unknown, but reports indicate he left the capital. The situation marks a dramatic and rapid change after 24 years of Assad’s leadership. Now, rebel groups will organize and select new leadership. This moment begins a new chapter for Syria, with hopes for stability after years of conflict. Difficult words: insurgent (a person who fights against a government), retreat (moving back or withdrawing), whereabouts (the place where someone or something is). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

President Bashar al-Assad of Syria left Damascus after rebels entered the city without much fighting. The rebels announced that Damascus is now free from Assad’s control. This happened just two weeks after they started their attacks in northern Syria. According to reports, the Syrian army told officers the regime fell. Prime Minister Mohammed al-Jal-Ali said he would help with a peaceful change of power. The Syrian people will choose the new leader. The rebels freed prisoners and met little opposition from the soldiers. Many Syrian soldiers ran away or crossed the border into Iraq. Assad’s location is unknown, and rebels now need to decide who will lead the country next. This is a big change after 24 years of Assad’s rule. Difficult words: rebel (a person who fights against the government), regime (a government), opposition (a conflict, or fight). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Rebels take over the city of Damascus. Syria’s President Bashar al-Assad leave the city. The rebels say that Damascus is now free. They start fighting in the north of Syria two weeks ago. They quickly move to the capital. Syria’s Prime Minister will help the people choose a new leader. The rebels free prisoners as they move into the city. Many soldiers run away or go to Iraq. There is little fighting. We do not know where Assad is. The rebels must now decide who will lead the country. This is the end of 24 years of Assad’s rule . Difficult words: rebel (a person who fights against the government), free (to let go), rule (control over an area or people). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

El Hierro, a small Canary Island, is struggling to cope with an unprecedented number of migrant deaths and disappearances. Forensic pathologist Modesto Martinez moved there hoping for a peaceful retirement but now works constantly due to the rise in migrant fatalities. In 2024, 33 migrants arrived dead or died shortly after arrival, compared to only 11 in 2023. The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands has become increasingly deadly, with more migrants missing or dying during the journey than before. Martinez identifies causes of death such as hypothermia , dehydration, and seawater ingestion. Confirming identities is challenging because migrants often discard identification to avoid deportation. The Red Cross assists in tracing families, but most deceased migrants remain unidentified. Despite new cadaver refrigerators, the island’s facilities are inadequate. The grave of one migrant, Bathie Barry, symbolizes the tragedy faced by thousands. Volunteers pay small tributes, showing empathy for those lost at sea. Difficult words: forensic pathologist (a medical doctor who investigates unexpected, or suspicious deaths), hypothermia (a dangerous drop in body temperature), cadaver (a dead body). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

El Hierro, a small Canary Island, is facing many problems because of migrant deaths and disappearances . Expert Modesto Martinez works hard to examine the bodies of migrants who die on the dangerous journey. This year, 33 migrants died in El Hierro, compared to 11 last year. Migrants take risky boat trips from West Africa, but many die from hypothermia or dehydration during the six-day journey. It is hard to identify the bodies because they throw away ID cards to avoid deportation. The Red Cross helps families find missing relatives, but most people remain unknown. Recently, a man named Bathie Barry died at sea. His grave is a symbol of the lost lives of migrants. Difficult words: disappearance (when someone goes missing), hypothermia (when the body temperature is too low), to avoid (to keep away from something or stop oneself from doing something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

On the small island of El Hierro, many migrants die or go missing. Expert Modesto Martinez checks the bodies of migrants who die after coming from West Africa. This year, 33 migrants die, which is more than last year. They die because they have no food, water, or shelter during the trip. Many migrants throw away their ID cards so that authorities do not send them back to their country. This makes it hard to know who they are. Some people put flowers on the grave of a migrant named Bathie Barry. They want to show respect for him and other migrants who die. Difficult words: shelter (a safe place to stay), ID card (a card with information on it, such as the name, date of birth, address, and so on), grave (a hole in the ground where we put a dead body). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

South Korea’s President Yoon Suk Yeol is being investigated for trying to declare martial law . Prosecutors accuse him of insurrection . Former Defense Minister Kim Yong-hyun, who resigned, is barred from leaving the country. Yoon’s impeachment is being debated. While his party, the People Power Party (PPP), opposes it, some members voted against his martial law order. Party leader Han Dong-hun called Yoon’s actions unconstitutional but warned that impeachment could create chaos. If impeached, the Prime Minister would lead until elections in 60 days. Amid the controversy , Yoon accepted Defense Minister Kim’s resignation and nominated Choi Byung-hyuk as his replacement. Several other ministers plan to resign. Yoon’s martial law lasted only hours after lawmakers in an emergency vote repealed it, even blocking troops from entering parliament. Difficult words: martial law (military control of government), insurrection (a violent uprising against an authority or government), controversy (a big debate over something), repeal (to remove the legal force of a law). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Authorities are investigating South Korea’s President Yoon Suk Yeol for trying to use martial law to take control of the country. Former Defense Minister Kim Yong-hyun, who suggested martial law, resigned and cannot leave the country. Yoon’s party doesn’t want impeachment , but some members don’t agree. If it happens, the Prime Minister will lead South Korea until the new elections. Yoon accepted Defense Minister Kim’s resignation and chose Choi Byung-hyuk to replace him. Other ministers may also quit. Yoon’s martial law lasted only a few hours. Lawmakers quickly voted to stop it and blocked soldiers from entering their building with furniture. Difficult words: martial law (when the military controls the country), impeachment (removing a leader of a country), resignation (leaving a job). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

South Korea’s President Yoon Suk Yeol tries to take control of the country. He uses martial law . It is a very serious crime called insurrection. Former Defense Minister Kim Yong-hyun comes with this idea. He quits his job and cannot leave the country. Some people in Yoon’s party do not agree with him. But they do not want to remove him as president yet. If Yoon ends, the Prime Minister will take over until new elections. Other government leaders may leave their jobs, too. Yoon’s martial law order lasts only a few hours. Lawmakers quickly vote to stop it. They use chairs to stop soldiers from coming into their building. Difficult words: martial law (when soldiers control the country), quit (to stop), remove (to take away). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, and his wife, Sheikha Jawaher, were welcomed on a state visit to the UK. King Charles and the Prince and Princess of Wales led the reception, with Prime Minister Keir Starmer also emphasizing Qatar’s importance in bilateral i nvestments and diplomacy. The Emir participated in ceremonial traditions at the Horse Guards Parade with Prince William and Princess Kate, marking her return to royal duties after preventive cancer treatment. Queen Camilla, recovering from pneumonia, attended the state banquet but skipped earlier outdoor ceremonies. King Charles highlighted Qatar’s leadership in peace efforts, clean energy, and investments while paying tribute to its role in global energy supply and humanitarian diplomacy . The banquet celebrated decades of UK-Qatar relations, strengthened by education, energy, and innovation. Difficult words: bilateral (involving two countries), preventive (done to stop something), diplomacy (managing international relations). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim, and his wife, Sheikha Jawaher, visited the UK. King Charles and Prince William welcomed them, along with Princess Kate, who returned to royal duties after cancer treatment . Prime Minister Keir Starmer also met the Emir to discuss investments. The Emir joined a ceremony at the Horse Guards Parade, but Queen Camilla skipped outdoor events because she was recovering from pneumonia . She later joined the state dinner. King Charles praised Qatar for helping with peace efforts and supporting clean energy projects. He said their visit supports the friendship between the two countries, which already work together in energy and science. Difficult words: treatment (medical care which a sick person gets), pneumonia (a lung illness), effort (hard work to achieve something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim, visits the UK with his wife, Sheikha Jawaher. King Charles, Prince William, and Princess Kate greet them. Kate is back at work after cancer treatmen t . Queen Camilla is getting better from a lung disease. She only joins the dinner later. King Charles thanks Qatar for helping with peace. The country also works hard on using clean energy. The visit shows the friendship between the UK and Qatar. The two countries are already working together in energy and science. Difficult words: cancer (a serious illness), treatment (medical care which a sick person gets), friendship (being close and kind to someone). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The Sydney Opera House, one of the world’s most recognizable buildings, is now a leader in sustainability at 51 years old. This UNESCO World Heritage site hosts 2,000 shows annually and attracts 11 million visitors. Behind the scenes, advanced technology monitors air quality, temperature, and energy usage. Over 1,400 sensors gather data, optimizing conditions every 15 minutes. For cooling, seawater from Sydney Harbor is used, reducing electricity consumption. The Opera House received a six-star certification from Green Building Council Australia for its sustainable efforts, including reducing energy and water use by 20% in five years. Despite its heritage status, requiring careful retrofitting , the building incorporates original eco-friendly designs like self-cleaning tiles and excellent drainage. To become carbon-positive by 2030, its operations ensure longevity. Staff consider themselves custodians, maintaining the structure for future generations. Software innovations also help monitor materials and manage repairs efficiently. Difficult words: sustainability (practices that protect the environment), optimize (make the best or most effective use of), retrofit (to add a component or accessory to something that didn’t have it when manufactured). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The Sydney Opera House is 51 years old and still famous for its unique design. It hosts many shows and visitors every year and is now more eco-friendly than ever. Technology helps manage air, temperature, and energy use. Over 1,400 sensors check data every 15 minutes. The building uses seawater from the harbor to cool rooms, which saves a lot of energy energy. The Opera House managed to cut energy and water use by 20% in five years. It cannot have solar panels because it is a heritage building , but original designs like rain-cleaning tiles and good drainage help. Workers are proud to care for the building and keep it ready for the future. Difficult words: eco-friendly (good for the planet), sensor (a small device which checks the temperature, pressure, or other things), heritage building (a building which is old and important). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The Sydney Opera House is 51 years old and very famous. It has many shows every year. Millions of people visit it every year. The building uses technology to save energy and keep visitors comfortable . Over 1,400 sensors check air and temperature often. Seawater from the harbor cools the building. It saves a lot of electricity. The Opera House is very green. It has many awards for using less energy and water. Its old design helps too. Workers take care of it and keep it safe for the future. The goal is to make the Opera House better for the planet by 2030. Difficult words: comfortable (feeling good), sensor (a tool which checks the temperature, pressure, or other things), award (a prize). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Cuba faced a major blackout when its national grid collapsed, leaving millions without power. By evening, only about 533 MW of electricity was generated, far below the 3,000 MW needed during peak demand. The government prioritized restoring power to hospitals and water systems, while schools and non-essential services remained closed. Power was partially restored in Havana, but over 260,000 homes remained in darkness. This crisis stems from the country’s aging power grid, worsened by fuel shortages, natural disasters, and economic challenges. Key power plants, including the Antonio Guiteras plant in Matanzas, were offline due to failures or maintenance. The shortage of oil imports from Venezuela, Russia, and Mexico has pushed Cuba’s oil-based plants into a deeper crisis. Citizens are frustrated by blackouts, food, water, and medicine shortages. In response, some protests have occurred. The government recently mandated businesses use renewable energy and reduce electricity consumption. Difficult words: prioritize (to treat something as being very important), stem from (to be caused by), mandate (to order officially). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Cuba had a big blackout that left millions without power. By the evening, power plants produced only 533 MW of electricity, far less than the 3,000 MW the country needed. The government said it would restore electricity to hospitals and water systems first, and schools stayed closed. In Havana, power returned to some homes, but many people were still without light. Old power systems, less fuel from other countries, and natural disasters cause these problems. The main power plant in Matanzas stopped working, and other plants were not ready. People in Cuba also don’t have enough food, water, and medicine, and they start to protest. The government now asks businesses to use renewable energy and reduce their power use. Difficult words: blackout (when homes and businesses are without electricity), restore (to bring back), renewable (when you can use something again). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Cuba has a power problem. Many people have no electricity. By the evening, only a little electricity is working. But the country needs much more. The government is fixing power for hospitals and water first. Schools must close. In Havana, some houses get power back, but many people stay in the dark. Cuba’s power system is very old. A big power plan t stops working. The country also has little fuel . This makes life hard, with little food, water, or medicine. Some people are angry and protesting. The government asks businesses to use green energy and use less power. Difficult words: power plant (a factory which makes electricity), fuel (material for making energy), green energy (energy from the sun, wind, and sea). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Thousands of protesters gathered in Tbilisi after Georgia’s government paused European Union EU accession talks until 2028. Demonstrators chanted ‘ traitors ’ and displayed photos of journalists allegedly harmed by police during earlier protests. Riot police used pepper spray and water cannons to disperse crowds, with reports of violent clashes and 43 arrests. Many journalists were injured. Over 100 diplomats and civil servants condemned the government’s decision, stating it contradicts Georgia’s strategic interests. The Prime Minister, Irakli Kobakhidze, justified the decision, accusing the EU of blackmail for questioning last month’s elections. Protests continued, and students, civil servants, and universities joined to express disapproval. Many see the government’s actions as aligning with Russia. The situation remains tense, with more demonstrations expected. Difficult words: accession (the process of joining an organization), traitor (a person who betrays someone or something), contradict (to go against). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

In Georgia’s capital, Tbilisi, thousands of people protested after the government delayed talks to join the EU until 2028. Police used pepper spray and water cannons and arrested 43 people. Many journalists got hurt, and some got hurt in previous protests already. Over 100 diplomats said the government doesn’t support Georgia’s goals, but the Prime Minister defended his decision. Protests continued, and students and workers joined them, too. Some schools and offices stopped working to show their disagreement . Many people believe the government is working with Russia rather than helping Georgia join the EU. Workers and journalists are planning more protests in the coming weeks. Difficult words: delay (to make something happen at a later time), defend (to speak for something), disagreement (a situation in which people don’t have the same opinion). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Tbilisi is Georgia’s capital. People in Tbilisi are upset . The government has stopped plans to join the EU until 2028. People protest. Police used pepper spray and water to stop the protests. Many people go to prison. Some journalists are hurt. Workers and students also join the protests. Some schools close because of this. The Prime Minister says that the EU is not unfair. The EU says that Georgia has problems in elections. Many people think that the government is working with Russia and not helping Georgia join the EU. More protests will happen soon. Difficult words: upset (angry, unhappy), join (to take part), journalist (a person who writes or talks about the news). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The town of Lustenau in Austria claims to have built a world-record-breaking bonfire. According to the organizers, the pyre reached as high as 60 meters. The structure took three months to build but collapsed in less than half an hour last Saturday evening. Embers from the big fire fell onto nearby market traders, but local fire crews were on hand to make sure that everyone was safe. Difficult words: claim (say), pyre (a tower of wood or something which you can set on fire), ember (a small piece of burning wood). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A town in Austria built the tallest pyre in the world. It took the people three months to build, and after they set it on fire, it collapsed in less than 30 minutes. The structure was 60 meters tall. Embers from the big fire flew everywhere, but local fire crews made sure that everyone was safe. Difficult words: pyre (a tower of wood which you set on fire), structure (something that you build), ember (a small piece of burning wood). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A town in Austria sets a world record. People build a 60-metre tower. It takes them three months. They build it from wood. They set this tower on fire. It becomes the biggest bonfire in the world. It collapses in 30 minutes. Fire crews are on site . They make sure that everybody is safe. Difficult words: bonfire (a large open-air fire; people burn it as part of a celebration), collapse (fall down), on site (there, in the area). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

During organized tours, tourists can visit a former Nazi compound 40 kilometers from Berlin called the ’Forbidden City’. Twenty thousand people visit near here every year to learn about Nazi military history. The Nazis and the Soviets were militarily active at the compound, which was kept secret in a forest and behind a fence. The Nazis hid underground bunkers in country homes, and they planned much of WWII here. After WWII, when the Soviet Union was in charge of East Germany, the Soviets used the complex as a home for 40,000 soldiers and as a cultural center with a theatre, a museum, shopping areas, and a swimming pool. In 1994, the Soviets left and took everything with them. The state of Brandenburg now owns the complex. Difficult words: compound (a series of buildings on one property and a wall around the property), former (existing in the past). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

In Germany, tourists can go on organized tours to visit a secret Nazi compound called the ‘Forbidden City’. Both the Nazis and the Soviets used the complex. The complex stayed secret inside of a forest and behind a fence. The Nazis hid underground bunkers in homes where they planned much of WWII here. After WWII, the Soviet Union was in charge of East Germany. The Soviet Union used the compound as a home for its 40,000 soldiers. In 1994, the Russians left and took everything with them. Difficult words: compound (a series of buildings in one area and a wall around all of it) , Soviets (the name for Russians when Russia was a communist country), bunker (a partly underground place for the army). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In Germany, tourists can see something new. They can see a secret Nazi compound called the ‘ Forbidden City’. They cannot go alone. They must go in groups with a guide. The compound is a secret in WWII. It is inside of a forest. It is behind a fence. The Nazis plan WWII there. They use the underground bunkers to hide. The Soviet Union is in charge of East Germany after WWII. The Soviet Union also uses the compound. Its 40,000 soldiers stay there. In 1994, the Soviets leave. They take everything. Difficult words: compound (a group of buildings in one area and a wall around all of it) , forbidden (you cannot see or visit something forbidden), bunker (a partly underground place for the army), the Soviet Union (Communist Russia). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Louis Vuitton is one of the most famous fashion brands; however, spotting a fake bag can be challenging. Scripps News reporter John Matarese demonstrated this difficulty while inspecting Louis Vuitton items. More people shop for designer bags during the holiday season, but counterfeit products are often sold online. Melanie McGovern from the Better Business Bureau advises checking websites carefully. If a site looks untrustworthy , has copied pictures, or offers prices too good to be true, it might be a scam. Buyers should also read reviews to see if others received their orders or had bad experiences. Even experienced shoppers can be tricked, as shown by Matarese’s test of identifying real and fake bags. He initially guessed wrong because small details, like stitching and materials, revealed the truth. Fake items often appear convincing but are poorly made and leave buyers feeling disappointed. Difficult words: counterfeit (fake), untrustworthy (not reliable or honest), initially (at first). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Louis Vuitton is a famous brand, but fake bags are hard to spot. Reporter John Matarese showed how tricky it can be while shopping. Many people want designer bags during the holidays, but some online stores sell fake products. It is important to check websites carefully. If the site has copied photos or low prices, it might not be real. Reading reviews can also help you know if people got their orders without problems. Matarese tried to guess which bag was fake and got it wrong! Small details like stitching and the material can show if it is real or not. Fakes might look good, but the quality is poor, so buyers feel unhappy. Difficult words: tricky (difficult), review (when someone gives their opinion about a book, film product, etc.), stitching (the thread which holds some materials together). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Louis Vuitton is a famous brand. But some bags are fake . Reporter John Matarese shows how hard it is to tell the difference. Many people buy bags for holidays. Australia has passed a law banning social media for anyone under 16. This law starts in late 2025 and targets platforms like Instagram, TikTok, and Snapchat, requiring them to prevent underage users or face fines of up to 49.5 million Australian dollars. The government acted because of widespread concern about social media’s harmful effects on children’s mental health, including cases of self-harm caused by bullying . While many parents and 77% of Australians support the ban, critics argue it might push young users to unsafe online spaces and teach them how to bypass restrictions. Child rights and privacy groups, along with some tech companies like Google and Meta, opposed the law. They say the bill was rushed, and methods for enforcing it are unclear. This legislation could strain Australia’s ties with the US and inspire similar laws globally. Difficult words: bullying (repetitive, intentional hurting of one person or group by another person or group), bypass (to avoid something), strain (to influence). The Electric Dreams exhibition at London’s Tate Modern celebrates the pioneers of digital art from the 1950s to the 1990s and explores the relationship between art and technology. The exhibition shows 150 works with artists using machines and algorithms to create art. The exhibition highlights early examples of machine-made art, like Harold Cohen’s abstract shapes, once dismissed as a fad . It also includes innovative paintings by Palestinian artist Samia Halaby, created on her home computer in the 1980s. Halaby’s work reflects her thoughts on contested lands, such as Palestine, showing how art intersects with social issues. Many technologies used in these artworks originally served military purposes. Instead of destruction, artists transformed them into tools for creation and offered a fresh perspective of technology in art. Artists had mixed feelings about technology’s positive and negative impacts, a sentiment that remains as debates around artificial intelligence and creativity intensify. Difficult words: pioneer (a person who is among the first to study or develop something), fad (a style, activity, or interest that is very popular for a short period), intersect (to meet or cross each other), sentiment (a view or opinion). American spending on iced coffee, cold brew , and frozen coffee drinks surged to over 17 billion dollars in 2023, doubling since 2016. Starbucks reported that cold drinks made up 76% of beverage sales in the third quarter of 2024. This reflects their growing popularity, especially among Gen Z and Millennials, who view cold coffee as an all-year beverage, breaking free from its traditional association with summer. Experts suggest that iced coffee’s appeal comes from its customization , the ability to mask its bitterness with flavors, and its aesthetic suitability for social media. Chains like Dunkin’ and Dutch Bros have also seen significant growth in cold drink sales. Cold coffee trends shape consumer habits, and they are reflected in at-home brewing practices. Although hot coffee remains the dominant choice, cold coffee is growing faster due to the influence of younger consumers and the American preference for experimentation, unlike traditional coffee cultures in Europe or South America. Difficult words: cold brew (chilled coffee made from grounds that have been steeped in cold water for several hours), appeal (the quality of being attractive or interesting), customization (making something unique to preferences). David Crisp, a British businessman, admitted on camera to selling luxury perfumes illegally in Russia, despite UK sanctions. In an undercover video, he confessed to ignoring government orders.
